claims.text: Applying spark plasma sintering to a lightweight high-entropy alloy produces a dual-phase microstructure.
Rapid SPS processing induces nanoscale secondary precipitates within a low-density matrix.
The SPS-induced precipitates improve mechanical strength relative to conventional sintering.
The SPS-induced precipitates improve corrosion resistance relative to conventional sintering.
The SPS-induced precipitates improve high-temperature oxidation resistance relative to conventional sintering.
The initial as-cast or conventionally sintered alloy has a relatively homogeneous, single-phase microstructure.
Optimized high heating rates, short dwell times, and rapid cooling promote nanoscale precipitate formation without significantly changing the alloy's low density.
The alloy composition must intrinsically support precipitation under rapid thermal processing conditions.
SPS forms a fine dispersion of nanoscale secondary precipitates at grain boundaries or within the matrix.
The nanoscale secondary precipitates reinforce the alloy.
Rapid SPS thermal cycles accelerate diffusion and nucleation, causing secondary precipitate formation.
Secondary precipitates increase strength by impeding dislocation motion.
Secondary precipitates act as barriers to corrosive degradation.
Secondary precipitates act as barriers to oxidative degradation.
The SPS-treated alloy will have a statistically significant increase in yield strength relative to the conventionally sintered baseline.
The SPS-treated alloy will have lower corrosion current density than the conventionally sintered baseline.
The SPS-treated alloy will have lower high-temperature oxidation weight gain than the conventionally sintered baseline.
The SPS-treated alloy will retain a low overall density.
Insufficiently rapid cooling will leave the microstructure homogeneous and prevent the predicted property improvements.
A composition not conducive to precipitation will leave the microstructure homogeneous and prevent the predicted property improvements.
